segments.text: There is a massive flood of opinions about artificial intelligence right now.
You see them constantly on TikTok, on the evening news, and in your family group chats.
With all that noise, it's hard to figure out whose predictions actually carry any weight.
To cut through the static, we can look directly at the people who build these massive systems for a living.
They are looking at the exact same data we are, but they are drawing wildly different conclusions.
Same field, same evidence.
Very different bets.
Look at this board breaking down two major players in the field.
On the left is Dario Amadei.
He helped build GPT-2 and GPT-3 at OpenAI, and now runs anthropic.
He's an optimist.
He says, AI-enabled biology and medicine will allow us to compress the progress that human biologists would have achieved over the next 50-100 years into five to ten years.
Yet even he acknowledges the immense risk.
He admits, humanity is about to be handed almost unimaginable power, and it is deeply unclear whether our social, political, and technological systems possess the maturity to wield it.
Now look at the right side.
Jeffrey Hinton is a warrior.
He won a Nobel Prize for the foundational ideas behind AI, and recently left his job at Google specifically to warn the public about its dangers.
He says, we're actually making new kinds of beings.
They have goals.
We give them goals, and from those goals, they derive other goals.
We don't necessarily know what other goals they'll derive.
But his outlook isn't entirely dark.
He also admits, if we can detect cancer much earlier thanks to AI, fewer people will die from it.
Notice the overlap here.
The optimist sees severe danger, and the warrior sees massive potential benefits.
None of them has a simple one-sided view.
That tells us something important.
Even the people who know this technology best don't know exactly where it's heading.
Where AI will be in ten years is a bet.
If top experts can't predict the future, you shouldn't feel pressured to figure it out either.
Even the experts disagree about where AI is going.
What's actually in your hands?
That's where to put your energy.
Looking at this chart, you see a clear divide.
Surviving means letting go of things you can't control, and committing entirely to skills you can build today.
It's out of your hands how AI changes future jobs.
What is in your hands is choosing to build real depth in a subject you actually care about.
You can't control how quickly AI changes.
You can, however, stay curious and keep using the specific tools that work.
Forget worrying about how much work AI produces.
Instead, focus your energy on practicing and coming up with original ideas.
You have no say in how other people use AI, but you have complete agency over how you choose to use it,
and how you work alongside others.
Finally, you can't predict what the next headline will say, but you can start making something real instead of waiting.
The bottom line of this board is straightforward.
You don't control every outcome, but your choices still matter.
Keep informed about the left column. Put most of your energy into the right.
As this final graphic shows, you can't control where AI goes next.
You can build the skill and judgment to decide what you do next.
